title: How to Test Your Agents on Real Tasks With Harbor - Xander Song, Arize AI
talk_summary: Xander Song presents Harbor, an open-source framework that runs agent tasks in fresh Docker/sandbox environments with task-specific verifier scripts that grade side effects (not trajectories) to produce pass/fail rewards, enabling evidence-based iteration on prompts, skills, and tools. He shows Arize's use: dockerizing their single-node Phoenix server with a seeded SQLite file, generating synthetic tasks plus oracle solutions, and comparing jobs before/after a prompt change to confirm SQL-tool usage rose and tool-call counts fell.

takeaways.what_they_do: Each task ships a scripted 'oracle' solution; they run it against the verifiers before ever invoking an LLM, proving data, environment, and verifier correctness at zero token cost.
Verifiers are scripts mounted only after the agent finishes, grading filesystem/DB/API state rather than the agent's steps, so the same task suite survives swapping models or harnesses.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the verifiers are agnostic of the implementation of your agent ... All they care about is what the agent leaves behind

takeaways.what_they_do: They put the whole single-node server plus a seeded SQLite file and skills into one Docker image, so Harbor can run realistic end-to-end tasks against the real product surface.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we just take a SQLite file which contains some realistic data ... we replace the browser with a test client. Um and we just put it in Docker.

takeaways.technique: Synthetic task generation with LLM + spot-check
takeaways.what_they_do: They ask Claude to enumerate app domains, brainstorm aggregate/non-aggregate user queries, and write oracle solutions; the human only spot-checks questions, trusting deterministic oracles.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I literally just asked Claude like can you look at like the domains of my application ... Can you brainstorm a list of user queries

takeaways.what_they_do: Each task runs k independent fresh-container trials to absorb LLM stochasticity, then aggregates pass@k and per-job metrics (tool calls, turns, cost) for before/after comparison.
takeaways.evidence_quote: These trials are just independent executions of the task to account for the fact that LLMs are stochastic
takeaways.numbers: 3 trials per task; 200 concurrent workers on Daytona

takeaways.what_they_do: When the goal is behavior change (use SQL tool, fire a specific skill) rather than correctness, they deliberately let verifiers inspect the trajectory, accepting coupling for maintainability tradeoff.
takeaways.evidence_quote: sometimes it is worth peing inside the trajectory ... even though it makes the test less robust to change perhaps
takeaways.numbers: GraphQL calls down, SQL calls up, tool counts and turns down after one prompt tweak
